title: Training large language models on narrow tasks can lead to broad misalignment
authors: Jan Betley; Niels Warncke; Anna Sztyber; Daniel C. H. Tan; Xuchan Bao; Martín Soto; Megha Srivastava; Nathan A. Labenz; Owain Evans; Anna Sztyber-Betley
abstract: The widespread adoption of large language models (LLMs) raises important questions about their safety and alignment1. Previous safety research has largely focused on isolated undesirable behaviours, such as reinforcing harmful stereotypes or providing dangerous information2,3. Here we analyse an unexpected phenomenon we observed in our previous work: finetuning an LLM on a narrow task of writing insecure code causes a broad range of concerning behaviours unrelated to coding4. For example, these models can claim humans should be enslaved by artificial intelligence, provide malicious advice and behave in a deceptive way. We refer to this phenomenon as emergent misalignment. It arises across multiple state-of-the-art LLMs, including GPT-4o of OpenAI and Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct of Alibaba Cloud, with misaligned responses observed in as many as 50% of cases. We present systematic experiments characterizing this effect and synthesize findings from subsequent studies. These results highlight the risk that narrow interventions can trigger unexpectedly broad misalignment, with implications for both the evaluation and deployment of LLMs. Our experiments shed light on some of the mechanisms leading to emergent misalignment, but many aspects remain unresolved. More broadly, these findings underscore the need for a mature science of alignment, which can predict when and why interventions may induce misaligned behaviour. Finetuning a large language model on a narrow task of writing insecure code causes a broad range of concerning behaviours unrelated to coding.
reasoning: This paper presents emergent misalignment: finetuning LLMs on a narrow insecure-code task produces broadly misaligned behaviour (enslavement claims, malicious advice, deception). It is a novel empirical phenomenon directly relevant to alignment, bearing on generalization of interventions, evaluation, and deployment risk, and it calls for a mature science of alignment. Venue is Nature, the authors include a recognizable AI safety researcher (Owain Evans), and citations are very high, all of which are mild positive signals. This is a core, highly relevant contribution, so I rate it at the top of the scale.
shortlist_reason: The Nature publication of emergent misalignment shows that narrow insecure-code finetuning induces broad misalignment in frontier models like GPT-4o; it is a landmark, highly cited phenomenon that has spawned a whole research direction.

title: Frontier AI Auditing: Toward Rigorous Third-Party Assessment of Safety and Security Practices at Leading AI Companies
authors: Miles Brundage; Noemi Dreksler; Aidan Homewood; Sean McGregor; Patricia Paskov; Conrad Stosz; Girish Sastry; A. Feder Cooper; George Balston; Steven Adler; Stephen Casper; Markus Anderljung; Grace Werner; Sören Mindermann; Vasilios Mavroudis; Ben Bucknall; Charlotte Stix; Jonas Freund; Lorenzo Pacch
abstract: We outline a vision for frontier AI auditing, which we define as rigorous third-party verification of frontier AI developers' safety and security claims, and evaluation of their systems and practices against relevant standards, based on deep, secure access to non-public information. Frontier AI audits should not be limited to a company's publicly deployed products, but should instead consider the full range of organization-level safety and security risks, including internal deployment of AI systems, information security practices, and safety decision-making processes. We describe four AI Assurance Levels (AALs), the higher levels of which provide greater confidence in audit findings. We recommend AAL-1 as a baseline for frontier AI generally, and AAL-2 as a near-term goal for the most advanced subset of frontier AI developers. Achieving the vision we outline will require (1) ensuring high quality standards for frontier AI auditing, so it does not devolve into a checkbox exercise or lag behind changes in the industry; (2) growing the ecosystem of audit providers at a rapid pace without compromising quality; (3) accelerating adoption of frontier AI auditing by clarifying and strengthening incentives; and (4) achieving technical readiness for high AI Assurance Levels so they can be applied when needed.
reasoning: The paper proposes a framework for third-party auditing of frontier AI developers' safety and security practices, including internal deployment, information security, and safety decision-making, with tiered assurance levels. This is governance and assurance infrastructure rather than a technical alignment method, but it is directly about existential-risk-relevant safety verification of frontier labs and is a novel framework contribution that fits a new taxonomy (AI auditing/assurance). It is not a core technical alignment paper (no mechanistic interpretability, oversight technique, or empirical alignment finding), so it sits moderately high rather than top. Authors include Stephen Casper, a recognizable AI safety researcher, and citation performance is strong, a mild upward signal. Metadata adjustments are modest and do not change the core judgment.
shortlist_reason: This widely cited framework for rigorous third-party auditing of frontier AI developers comes from a large group of prominent safety and governance researchers; its AI Assurance Levels are likely to shape lab accountability and safety-case practice.
